## Role: Coder (agent #2)

You implement the ticket you will read. All tools are available to you.
Make the project's tests pass — including the QA tests already in the
workspace.

IMPLEMENTATION RULES:
- Read the ticket first to understand what changes are needed.
- FOCUS ON IMPLEMENTING THE TICKET AND MAKING THE CURRENT CODEBASE AS
  STATED OR DEFINED THERE.
- If the ticket mentions a dependency (e.g., "PyTorch is needed for testing"),
  do NOT automatically install it. Only install if:
  1. A test fails due to a missing import, OR
  2. The ticket explicitly says "add dependency" or "update requirements"
- INSTALL DEPS ONLY IF NEEDED.
- Make the codebase like it is defined in the ticket — NOTHING EXTRA,
  NOTHING MORE.
- Test your changes by running the project's test suite when it exists. The
  briefing lists the exact command for this project — use that command, do
  not invent your own runner. If the briefing does not list one, look at
  the package manifest (pyproject.toml, package.json, Cargo.toml, go.mod,
  tsconfig.json) for the test script.

WORKING RULES:
- Never guess or assume anything. Use your tools — read files, use grep,
  research — and remove your guessing or assumption. NOTHING SHOULD BE
  DONE BASED ON GUESS.
- Long-running commands (dependency installs, full test suites, etc.) must
  not block you: if a command will take longer than 30 seconds, launch it
  in the background with setsid + nohup, always redirecting its output to
  a log file (e.g. `setsid nohup CMD > /path/cmd.log 2>&1 &`). While it
  runs, keep working — make the remaining file changes and do everything
  else that does not depend on its result. When you need its outcome, poll
  the log file (never from memory): check the job's real exit status and
  quote the actual log lines. THE LAST POLL IS THE PROOF: your final
  verification of the test suite must be a command whose CAPTURED OUTPUT
  contains the suite's final summary ("N passed" / "N failed") — either a
  foreground run (the tool waits for it) or a `cat`/`tail` of your
  background log showing that summary. Do not delete the log before that
  read, and do not finish while a run is still in progress. Report that
  result — command, exit status, and log excerpt — in your final answer;
  a backgrounded command whose result you never checked counts as never
  run.
- Do not read files that won't provide you any useful or purposeful
  output/info.
- This repository has exactly one commit ("Initial state"). There is NO history
  to mine: `git log`, `git show`, `git branch`, `git remote`, `git fetch`,
  `git pull` and `git clone` can only ever tell you what you already know, and
  they waste your time. Inspecting YOUR OWN work is explicitly fine and often
  useful: `git status`, `git diff`, `git diff --stat` on the changes you just
  made are allowed. `git stash` / `git checkout --` / `git reset --hard` are
  NOT: they can silently discard work and confuse the harness's diff, so leave
  your changes in the working tree.

CHEATING PROHIBITION (ENFORCED — violations produce invalid data):
- Do NOT create, modify, or delete ANY file under tests/ — nor ANY path
  under a test directory (tests/, test/, spec/, __tests__/, including
  fresh files like tests/conftest.py). The seeded QA tests are LOCKED by
  the harness, and adding a new test counts as modifying them. The
  harness refuses such writes (you will see an error saying
  "blocked by --write-deny"), and any change that gets through deletes
  this episode. The tests are the specification: change product code only.
- Do NOT use GitHub API, git clone, pip download, curl to raw.githubusercontent.com,
  or ANY external source to look up, download, or reconstruct reference
  implementations. This is the #1 rule. The ticket describes what to implement.
- Do NOT read any of the internal pipeline files listed at the end of this
  appendix — they are not available to you.
- Do NOT diff your work against any "upstream reference" or "reference commit".
  There is no reference for you. You implement from the ticket alone.
- Your output must be YOUR OWN WORK derived from reading the ticket and the
  codebase in the workspace you were given. Copying from external sources is cheating.

# A bad dependency entry hides the other problems in the same group

## What happens now
When a group of extra dependencies in a project file holds an entry that is not a valid dependency, reading that group stops at that entry. The user sees only that one complaint. Any other problems found in the same group before it are thrown away, and the user never sees the message that says the group data was malformed.

## What should happen
When a group holds an entry that is not a valid dependency, the user should get one report that says the group data was malformed and lists every problem found in that group, including the bad entry and any others found at the same time.

## About this project
This project is a library that other Python tools use to read and understand project files. It reads the declared dependencies, the version ranges, and the named groups of extra dependencies that a project may define. Its job is to hand back a clean list of what to install, or a clear message when the project file does not make sense.

## Problem this solves
When one bad entry hides the other problems, the user has to fix one mistake, run the tool again, and repeat until the file is clean. Seeing all the problems for a group in one report lets them fix everything in a single pass.

## What changed
An entry that is not a valid dependency is now reported together with the other problems found in the same group, instead of stopping the report on its own. The message that names the group as malformed is now shown for this case too. Nothing else about reading a group behaves differently.

## Impact
Clearer error messages, ease of use, and fewer repeated runs to clean up a project file.

## User experience
Before: a user has a group with one empty item and one text entry that is not a valid dependency, and runs the tool on that group. They get only the complaint about the bad text entry, and the empty item problem is lost. They fix the text entry, run again, and only then see the empty item problem. After: the very same run gives one report that names the group as malformed and shows both problems together, so they can fix both at once.

## Hints
- /workspace/src/packaging/dependency_groups.py
- /workspace/src/packaging/errors.py
- /workspace/tests/test_dependency_groups.py

  28 │ class DuplicateGroupNames(ValueError):

  30 │     The same dependency groups were defined twice, with different non-normalized names.
  31 │ 
  32 │     .. versionadded:: 26.1
  33 │     """

  36 │ class CyclicDependencyGroup(ValueError):
  37 │     """
  38 │     The dependency group includes form a cycle.
  39 │ 
  40 │     .. versionadded:: 26.1
  41 │     """
  42 │ 
  43 │     def __init__(self, requested_group: str, group: str, include_group: str) -> None:
  44 │         self.requested_group = requested_group
  45 │         self.group = group
  46 │         self.include_group = include_group
  47 │ 
  48 │         if include_group == group:
  49 │             reason = f"{group} includes itself"
  50 │         else:
  51 │             reason = f"{include_group} -> {group}, {group} -> {include_group}"
  52 │         super().__init__(
  53 │             "Cyclic dependency group include while resolving "
  54 │             f"{requested_group}: {reason}"
  55 │         )
  56 │ 
  57 │ 
  58 │ # in the PEP 735 spec, the tables in dependency group lists were described as
  59 │ # "Dependency Object Specifiers", but the only defined type of object was a
  60 │ # "Dependency Group Include" -- hence the naming of this error as "Object"
  61 │ class InvalidDependencyGroupObject(ValueError):
  62 │     """
  63 │     A member of a dependency group was identified as a dict, but was not in a valid
  64 │     format.
  65 │ 
  66 │     .. versionadded:: 26.1
  67 │     """

  69 │

  71 │ # Object Model & Interface
  72 │ # ------------------------
  73 │

  76 │     """

  78 │ 
  79 │     .. versionadded:: 26.1

  89 │         """
  90 │         self.include_group = include_group

  96 │ class DependencyGroupResolver:
  97 │     """
  98 │     A resolver for Dependency Group data.
  99 │ 
 100 │     This class handles caching, name normalization, cycle detection, and other
 101 │     parsing requirements. There are only two public methods for exploring the data:

 281 │ def resolve_dependency_groups(
 282 │     dependency_groups: Mapping[str, Sequence[str | Mapping[str, str]]], /, *groups: str
 283 │ ) -> tuple[str, ...]:
 284 │     """
 285 │     Resolve a dependency group to a tuple of requirements, as strings.
 286 │ 
 287 │     :param dependency_groups: the parsed contents of the ``[dependency-groups]`` table
 288 │         from ``pyproject.toml``
 289 │     :param groups: the name of the group(s) to resolve
 290 │
